Collect a query and order it by the primary key of its table

Source: R/util_setorder_by_pk.R
collect_and_sort_by_pk.Rd

collect_and_sort_by_pk() replaces dplyr::collect() for a query that starts at DBTable_v9$tbl(). It returns a data.table, ordered by the primary key of that table and then by every other column.

Usage

collect_and_sort_by_pk(x)

Arguments

x

A lazy table that starts at DBTable_v9$tbl().

Value

A data.table with the rows of x, sorted as described in Details.

Details

PostgreSQL returns rows in no fixed order. The same query can return the same rows in a different order on each call. Code that reads d[1], d[.N] or tail(d, 1) after dplyr::collect() therefore gets an arbitrary row. collect_and_sort_by_pk() makes that row deterministic.

DBTable_v9$tbl() attaches the primary key of the table to the lazy table as the attribute csdb_pk. These dbplyr verbs keep the attribute on their result: filter(), select(), mutate(), group_by(), summarise(), arrange(), distinct(), head(), and left_join() and inner_join() on the x side.

The function sorts with setorder_by_pk(). The primary key columns that the result has come first, in primary key order. Every other column follows, in column order. A primary key column that a select() or a summarise() removed is not a sort column.

The attribute holds column names. After a rename() or a mutate() of a primary key column, the order is still fixed, but it is no longer the primary key order.

The sort runs after the collect. It cannot choose which rows a head() or another limit inside the query returns. Put a dplyr::arrange() before the limit when the rows matter.

The function stops with an error when x carries no primary key. It does not fall back to an unsorted collect. These are the causes:

  • the query did not start at DBTable_v9$tbl().

  • the table has no primary key, because its keys is NULL.

  • a step dropped the attribute, for example dplyr::compute(), or a join where the csdb table is on the y side.

For a result without a primary key, for example from DBI::dbGetQuery(), use setorder_by_pk() with table = NULL.

See also

Other row order: set_pk(), setorder_by_pk()

Examples

# \donttest{
# SQLite needs no server, so this block runs anywhere.
my_table <- DBTable_v9$new(
  dbconfig = list(driver = "SQLite", db = tempfile(fileext = ".sqlite")),
  table_name = "my_data_table",
  field_types = c("id" = "INTEGER", "week" = "INTEGER", "n" = "DOUBLE"),
  keys = c("id", "week")
)
my_table$insert_data(data.table::data.table(
  id = c(2L, 1L, 2L, 1L),
  week = c(2L, 2L, 1L, 1L),
  n = c(4, 3, 2, 1)
))
#> Creating table my_data_table

d <- my_table$tbl() |>
  dplyr::filter(id == 1L) |>
  collect_and_sort_by_pk()

# The last row is the last week of id 1, on every database.
d[.N]
#>       id  week     n
#>    <int> <int> <num>
#> 1:     1     2     3

my_table$disconnect()
# }
